trials.name: Clarity AD
trials.population: Participants with early Alzheimer's disease (MCI or mild dementia) with confirmed amyloid pathology
trials.primary_endpoint: Change from Baseline in the CDR-SB at 18 Months
trials.results_summary: Lecanemab significantly reduced brain amyloid burden and slowed cognitive and functional decline by 27% on the CDR-SB compared to placebo over 18 months. ARIA occurred more frequently in treated patients, particularly ApoE ε4 homozygotes.

trials.name: Study 201
trials.population: Subjects with early Alzheimer's disease (MCI or mild dementia) with confirmed amyloid pathology
trials.primary_endpoint: Core Study Phase: Change From Baseline in Alzheimer's Disease Composite Score (ADCOMS) at Month 12
trials.results_summary: Lecanemab showed a dose-dependent reduction in amyloid plaques and a trend toward slower clinical decline, which informed the selection of the 10 mg/kg biweekly dose for Phase 3 trials.

trials.primary_endpoint: AUC, Cmax, Tmax, and t1/2 of lecanemab
trials.results_summary: Demonstrated bioequivalence between the subcutaneous formulation of lecanemab supplied in vials versus a single-use auto-injector.

related_evidence.description: NEJM publication of Phase 3 Clarity AD primary results demonstrating slowed cognitive decline and amyloid clearance.
Alzheimer's Research & Therapy publication of Phase 2b proof-of-concept trial (Study 201) results.

evidence_assessment: Lecanemab's clinical efficacy and safety are well-supported by two rigorous, double-blind trials: the Phase 3 Clarity AD (NCT03887455) and the Phase 2b Study 201 (NCT01767311). Both studies conclusively show robust, dose-dependent clearance of brain amyloid plaques accompanied by a modest but statistically significant slowing of cognitive decline (27% on the CDR-SB over 18 months in Clarity AD). However, the clinical evidence reveals a challenging risk-benefit profile for ApoE ε4 homozygotes; despite effective amyloid clearance, exploratory analyses in this high-risk subgroup failed to show significant clinical benefit on the primary endpoint, while the incidence of ARIA was markedly higher (45% vs. 19% in heterozygotes). The newly added subcutaneous maintenance dosing option is grounded in Phase 1 bioequivalence data and open-label extensions, though the document appropriately limits claims regarding the long-term clinical benefit and safety of transitioning to this maintenance regimen.
discrepancies: The document states Study 2 evaluated 1,795 patients, while the ClinicalTrials.gov record for NCT03887455 lists an enrollment of 1,906. This is expected as 1,795 reflects the modified intention-to-treat population evaluated for efficacy, whereas 1,906 is the total randomized enrollment.

The document describes a subcutaneous injection maintenance option; this was not evaluated in the core 18-month placebo-controlled periods of Study 1 or Study 2, but rather in separate bioequivalence bridging studies (such as Phase 1 NCT05533801) and open-label extension cohorts.
